children: Shree Refrigerations’ R.G. Shende says mission-critical indigenisation demands years of demonstrated performance on board naval vessels, steady servicing and a willingness to build Navy feedback into product upgrades

India’s defence indigenisation push has moved from policy to practice, but the real test lies in the small and mid-sized firms that supply the “invisible” subsystems inside large platforms. R.G. Shende, Chairman and Managing Director of Shree Refrigerations Limited (SRL), says his company developed air conditioning for Scorpene submarines without foreign collaboration. In this interview, he explains what it takes to earn the Indian Navy’s trust, why infrastructure and test facilities must come before orders, and why policy should reserve MSME benefits for companies with at least 51 per cent local ownership.

India has set ambitious goals for defence indigenisation and exports, backed by positive indigenous lists and rising capital budgets. How far has the country come in building real domestic capability, as opposed to assembling imported systems, and where is the gap still widest?

For a country that builds rockets and all the high-tech equipment, defence indigenisation comes naturally and without much technological challenge. All it needed was governmental buying and support for indigenisation by way of negative lists and mandatory local content. Although some equipment needs to be imported due to economic considerations, most manufacturing and integration can be local, cutting dependence on foreign tech.

The government also supports tech development through the indigenisation push in schemes such as iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) and ADITI (Acing Development of Innovative Technologies with iDEX). Tech support is also available from DRDO by way of Transfer of Technology (ToT) to private enterprises. Patient capital is also made available for innovation funding. The results are there to be seen. In our own case, we were able to develop ACs for Scorpene submarines without any foreign collaboration.

Large defence platforms are built on the work of hundreds of specialised suppliers, many of them small and mid-sized, in areas such as cooling, controls and fabrication. Why do these “invisible” subsystems matter so much to a platform’s performance, and are they getting the attention and support they deserve?

Definitely. Dependence on foreign vendors needs to be reduced to a minimum to avoid a big drain on forex outflow. Quality control by the Director General of Quality Control (DGQA) ensures that the equipment is up to the exacting standards of workmanship and quality. All this happens at a fraction of the cost of imported equipment and service. Besides, post-installation service is also available locally and is highly price competitive.

Replacing an imported subsystem with an Indian-made one demands engineering depth, testing and years of trust-building with the Indian Navy. What does it actually take to indigenise a mission-critical system, and what do people outside the industry underestimate?

Perseverance, patience and focus are needed to demonstrate a firm’s commitment to serving the Navy. The firm has to establish credentials that take years to build and moments to lose. That is where the promoter’s (and his team’s) integrity and firm commitment matter. This is not for the faint-hearted. The ability to develop tech, demonstrate it on board naval vessels over a longer duration, service it over the years, and integrate Naval feedback into product upgrades are the important aspects.

Naval platforms need cooling and climate control that works in extreme heat, humidity, vibration and confined spaces, while energy efficiency and reliability are rising priorities. Which technologies will shape the next generation of marine and defence HVAC, and how ready is India to build them at home?
The focus here is more on stealth, reliability and serviceability. All the tech is available within India. Firms only have to rise to the occasion, bring out their best and deliver.

You spent over two decades in commercial refrigeration and air conditioning before turning towards defence. What did you have to unlearn, build or invest in to make that shift, and what advice would you give mid-sized industrial companies considering the same path?

Have heart, believe in yourself, ensure deep pockets and go for it. More importantly, invest in infra, registrations and a test facility before expecting any order. These are prerequisites and not something to be done “after I get the order”. The advantage here is long-term visibility of business, which allows you to build capacity and capability ahead of the market opportunity.

Defence manufacturing involves long approval cycles, rigorous qualification and large working-capital needs, and public markets are now showing strong interest in the sector. How should mid-sized defence suppliers balance patient, long-gestation growth with the expectations of investors?
Efficiency. That’s it. Invest in modernisation, better project execution capability, lower cash cycles and a strong order book. If the forces have faith in you, investors will.

India’s defence ecosystem is opening up to private players of all sizes, yet procurement processes remain demanding and slow for newcomers. What reforms would do the most to bring more capable private manufacturers into the supply chain and keep them there?

The government has done enough. It is time for Indian industry to rise to the occasion and demonstrate its skills and commitment. There is some scope for improvement in expediting payments, especially to MSMEs; this, over and above the TReDS channel, will help. The anomaly is that large foreign OEMs open a small office in India, harvest the local supply chains, become MSMEs in India and enjoy all the benefits of a local MSME. These firms have access to large overseas funds and can easily leverage their foreign clout to outbid a local MSME. The challenge is that the equipment still has foreign IP. This is not in line with Aatmanirbhar Bharat, although it may qualify under the Make in India norms of x per cent local content. This defeats the spirit of Aatmanirbhar Bharat. Policymakers need to review the policy to ensure that the benefits are available to companies with a minimum of 51 per cent local ownership. This will ensure higher participation of Indian MSMEs in this national capability-building initiative.

Looking ahead 10 years, what would a self-reliant Indian defence supply chain look like, in terms of exports, technology ownership and the role of small and mid-sized companies, and what has to happen to get there?

Companies requiring after-sales service support will find it challenging to export to foreign nations. The business volume needs to justify creating a service infrastructure in the customer country. Also, most countries would like to emulate their own version of “Make in My Country”. Exports are possible by way of JVs with local companies. Again, companies need to create that level of credibility. They also need to exhibit at foreign expos and trade shows, and demonstrate their capability, reference list, infrastructure and service capability at short notice. Again, build credibility and trust. This is a long process and there are no shortcuts.
Savi Khanna
BW Reporters Assistant Editor, BW Businessworld
